options.html: DMA requires a special controller that facilitates the transfer of blocks between the I/O device and main memory.
The overhead of polling depends on the polling frequency.
Polling is often a viable option for slow and asynchronous devices.
DMA usually slows down overall system performance.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, B

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Let's evaluate each statement:

A. DMA requires a special controller that facilitates the transfer of blocks between the I/O device and main memory.

✅ True

  • DMA (Direct Memory Access) uses a DMA controller (DMAC) to transfer data directly between an I/O device and main memory, reducing CPU involvement.

B. The overhead of polling depends on the polling frequency.

✅ True

  • Polling requires the CPU to repeatedly check device status.

  • If polling is done more frequently, CPU overhead increases.

  • Hence, the overhead depends on the polling frequency.

C. Polling is often a viable option for slow and asynchronous devices.

❌ False

  • Slow and asynchronous devices are generally better handled using interrupts, since polling would waste CPU cycles checking devices that are rarely ready.

  • Polling is more suitable for devices that need frequent servicing or where low latency is required.

D. DMA usually slows down overall system performance.

❌ False

  • DMA generally improves overall system performance by freeing the CPU from handling every data transfer.

  • Although DMA may temporarily contend for memory bandwidth ("cycle stealing"), it does not usually slow down the system overall.

Correct Answer: A and B ✅

options.html: Direct Memory Access (DMA) bypasses the cache or TLB to read directly from main memory.
Direct Memory Access (DMA) is "direct" because it accesses devices via memory directly rather than processor instructions.
Direct Memory Access (DMA) can reduce the load on the processor when accessing block devices such as disks.

When a DMA controller needs to use the bus to access memory, it performs "cycle stealing" by making the CPU wait if it is also trying to access memory. Even though the CPU is continually executing, the DMA device might find the bus to memory free when it needs to access memory.

questions.solution:
Answer: C, D

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

The correct choices are:

  • C. True

  • D. True

  • B. False

  • A. Generally considered false (or at least not universally true).

Here's why:

A. ❌ False (or not generally correct)

DMA bypasses the cache or TLB to read directly from main memory.

  • DMA does not use the CPU's TLB because it uses physical addresses (or an IOMMU if present).

  • However, saying it bypasses the cache is not always true. On many modern systems, DMA can be cache-coherent, meaning it interacts with the cache hierarchy rather than simply bypassing it.

  • Therefore, as written, this statement is too broad.

B. ❌ False

DMA is "direct" because it accesses devices via memory directly rather than processor instructions.

This is not what "Direct Memory Access" means. DMA is "direct" because data is transferred directly between an I/O device and main memory without the CPU copying each word or byte. The CPU only sets up the transfer.

C. ✅ True

DMA can reduce the load on the processor when accessing block devices such as disks.

Correct. DMA allows devices like disks and network cards to transfer large blocks of data directly to/from memory, freeing the CPU to perform other work.

D. ✅ True

DMA uses cycle stealing by making the CPU wait if both need the memory bus. If the CPU is not using the bus, DMA can use it without stalling the CPU.

This accurately describes cycle stealing. DMA temporarily takes control of the memory bus when needed. If the CPU also needs the bus, it must wait; otherwise, DMA can transfer data while the CPU continues executing instructions that do not require memory access.

Final Answer:

✅ C and D

Official discussion page

options.html: Interrupt-driven I/O allows the CPU to perform useful work while the I/O is performed.
Memory-mapped I/O uses standard memory instructions such as load and store.
Memory-mapped I/O uses a distinct memory space separate from physical memory.
DMA passes data through a CPU register during I/O.

questions.solution:
Answer: C, D

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Let's evaluate each statement:

A. Interrupt-driven I/O allows the CPU to perform useful work while the I/O is performed.
✅ True.
With interrupt-driven I/O, the CPU starts the I/O operation and continues executing other instructions. When the I/O device is ready or completes, it interrupts the CPU.

B. Memory-mapped I/O uses standard memory instructions such as load and store.
✅ True.
In memory-mapped I/O, device registers are assigned addresses in the regular memory address space, so normal load/store instructions are used to access them.

C. Memory-mapped I/O uses a distinct memory space separate from physical memory.
❌ False.
This describes isolated (port-mapped) I/O, not memory-mapped I/O. In memory-mapped I/O, devices share the same address space as memory.

D. DMA passes data through a CPU register during I/O.
❌ False.
Direct Memory Access (DMA) transfers data directly between the I/O device and main memory without passing through CPU registers. The CPU only initializes the DMA controller and is notified upon completion.

Answer: C and D are false.

questions.html: Assume that for a single polling operation, a processor running at $1$ MHz takes $200$ cycles. A processor polls a printer $1000$ times per minute. What percentage of time does the processor spend in polling? (Round off to $2$ decimal places)
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Given:

  • Processor clock rate = 1 MHz = (1,000,000) cycles/second

  • Cycles per polling operation = 200 cycles

  • Polling frequency = 1000 times/minute

 

Step 1: Convert polling frequency to polls per second

1000 polls/minute = 1000 ÷ 60 = 16.67 polls/second

Step 2: Calculate cycles spent polling per second

Cycles spent polling per second = 16.67 × 200
                               = 3333.33 cycles/second

Step 3: Calculate the percentage of CPU time spent polling

Percentage of CPU time = (3333.33 ÷ 1,000,000) × 100
                       = 0.3333%

Final Answer:
The processor spends approximately 0.33% of its time polling.

questions.html: With the GATE exam just a few months away, Alice realizes she won't finish making notes in time, so she buys a laser printer to print topper's handwritten notes. Suppose that she bought a laser printer that produces up to $45$ pages per minute, where each page consists of $5000$ characters. The manual for the laser printer states that the system uses interrupt-driven I/O by raising an interrupt for every character. If each interrupt takes $50$ microseconds to process, how much CPU time will be spent processing interrupts (in $\%$)?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Given:

  • Printing speed = 45 pages/min

 

  • Characters per page = 5000

 

  • One interrupt is generated for every character

 

  • Time taken to service one interrupt = 50 × 10⁻⁶ s 

 

  • Total CPU time considered = 60 s

 

 

Calculation:

Number of characters printed (and hence interrupts generated) in 1 minute:

45×5000=225000 interrupts

Total time spent servicing interrupts:

225000 × 50 × 10−6 = 11.25 s

Fraction of CPU time spent handling interrupts:

11.2560 / 60=0.875

Percentage of CPU time spent on interrupts:

0.1875×100=18.75%

Answer: 18.75%​ of the CPU time is spent servicing interrupts.

questions.html: Suppose Bob (a sneaky prankster) replaces Alice's laser printer with a toaster on April $1^{st}$. Unfortunately, Alice urgently needs to print lecture notes for the upcoming class, and decides that the easiest solution is to buy a new printer. The new printer has the same specifications as Alice's old printer: it can produce $45$ pages per minute, where each page consists of $5000$ characters. However, an upgrade in the system hardware allows the polling-driven implementation to take up only $10 \%$ of the CPU time instead. How long (in microseconds) should the interrupt-driven implementation take for each interrupt to "break even"? (Round off to $2$ decimal places.)
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Assuming:

  • CPU clock rate = 1 MHz = 1,000,000 cycles/second

  • Polling implementation uses 10% of CPU time

  • Printer speed = 45 pages/minute

  • Characters per page = 5000

  • One interrupt is generated per character printed

Step 1: Calculate characters printed per second

Characters/minute = 45 × 5000
                  = 225,000 characters/minute

Characters/second = 225,000 ÷ 60
                  = 3,750 characters/second

Step 2: Calculate CPU time available for interrupts

10% of CPU time = 10% × 1,000,000 cycles/second
                = 100,000 cycles/second

Step 3: Calculate maximum cycles per interrupt

Cycles/interrupt = 100,000 ÷ 3,750
                 = 26.67 cycles

Step 4: Convert cycles to time

At 1 MHz, one clock cycle = 1 μs.

Time per interrupt = 26.67 × 1 μs
                   = 26.67 μs

Final Answer

The interrupt-driven implementation should take approximately 26.67 μs per interrupt to break even with the polling implementation.

questions.html: Assume that a program wants to copy a $500$ word block of data from an I/O device to memory. Let $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}$ and C be the total number of READ I/O commands issued by the CPU to the I/O module using Programmed IO, Interrupt-driven IO and Direct-memory access respectively. What is the value of $A+B+C$ ?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

For a 500-word data transfer:

1. Programmed I/O

  • The CPU must issue one READ I/O command for each word.

  • Therefore,

    • A = 500

2. Interrupt-driven I/O

  • The CPU also issues one READ I/O command for each word.

  • After each word is ready, the device interrupts the CPU.

  • Therefore,

    • B = 500

3. Direct Memory Access (DMA)

  • The CPU issues one READ command to the DMA controller/I/O module to transfer the entire 500-word block.

  • The DMA controller then transfers all 500 words directly to memory.

  • Therefore,

    • C = 1

Calculate (A + B + C)

A = 500
B = 500
C = 1

A + B + C = 500 + 500 + 1
          = 1001

Final Answer:

1001

questions.html: A DMA module is transferring characters to memory using cycle stealing, from a device transmitting at $9600$ bps . The processor is fetching instructions at the rate of $1$ million instructions per second ( $1$ MIPS). By how much will the processor be slowed down due to the DMA activity (in $\%$)?
questions.solution:

Assume:

  • DMA transfer rate = 9600 bps

  • 1 character = 8 bits

  • Processor speed = 1 MIPS = 1,000,000 instructions/second

  • Cycle stealing: each DMA transfer steals one memory cycle, causing the CPU to lose the time for one instruction fetch.

Step 1: Calculate characters transferred per second

Characters/second = 9600 ÷ 8
                  = 1200 characters/second

Step 2: DMA memory cycles stolen per second

Each character transfer steals one memory cycle.

DMA cycles stolen/second = 1200

Step 3: Calculate processor slowdown

The CPU fetches:

1,000,000 instructions/second

The fraction of time lost is:

Slowdown = (1200 ÷ 1,000,000) × 100
         = 0.12%

Final Answer

The processor is slowed down by approximately 0.12%.

Answer: (0.12%)

questions.html: Consider a system in which bus cycles takes $500$ ns . Transfer of bus control in either direction, from processor to I/O device or vice versa, takes $250$ ns . One of the I/O devices has a data transfer rate of $50 \mathrm{~KB} / \mathrm{s}$ and employs DMA. Data are transferred 1 byte at a time. Suppose we employ DMA in a burst mode. That is, the DMA interface gains bus mastership prior to the start of a block transfer and maintains control of the bus until the whole block is transferred. For how long would the device tie up the bus when transferring a block of $128$ bytes?

options.html: $64.5$ microsecond
$64$ microsecond
$2.56$ millisecond
$3.56$ millisecond

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Concept Used here is as follow:

Bus Cycle: 500 ns

Here Bus Cycle means the amount of time taken to put the address on the bus, generate the appropriate control signals, and save/load data from/to memory.

Now the DMA first generates the handshaking signals for getting the bus control from the CPU. It takes 250 ns. Similarly, at the end, giving back the bus also takes 250 ns.

 

So we now know it takes 500 ns to take and release the bus.

 

As given in the question, 128 bytes of data are to be transferred.

 

We are also provided that 50 KB/s of data is generated by the I/O device constantly.

 

So, let us find the amount of time needed to generate 1 byte by the I/O device.

This turns out to be:

1 / (50 × 1024) s = 0.00001953125 s = 19531.25 ns

 

Now here is the main part.

The bus cycle time is 500 ns, whereas the time taken by the I/O device to generate 1 byte is 19531.25 ns.

Clearly, the bottleneck here is 19531.25 ns.

So, the time to transfer 128 bytes is:

 

Answer: 128 × 19531.25 ns + 500 ns = 2,500,500 ns = 2.50 ms ( if assume that the io gen data when the bus is used to transfer the data)

 

here we are using that when bus is used , io is not generating data (In this question if we do reverse engineering on ans)

 

time is 500 ns + 128 * (19531.25 + 500 ns) = 2.56 ms  (in the ans here with this assumption it is exactly 2.56 ms as we need to add 500 ns for the bus cycle as it is not overlaping)

 

 

The problem statement does not explicitly specify whether byte generation and bus transfer overlap. Therefore, the difference between 2.50 ms and 2.56 ms arises solely from this modeling assumption.

questions.html: Consider a system in which bus cycles takes $500$ ns . Transfer of bus control in either direction, from processor to I/O device or vice versa, takes $250$ ns . One of the I/O devices has a data transfer rate of $50 \mathrm{~KB} / \mathrm{s}$ and employs DMA. Data are transferred $1$ byte at a time. Suppose we employ DMA in a cycle-stealing mode. For how long (in microsecond) would the device tie up the bus when transferring a block of $128$ bytes?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Let's solve it step by step.

Given

  • Bus cycle time = 500 ns

  • Bus control transfer (CPU ↔ DMA) = 250 ns each way

  • DMA mode = Cycle stealing

  • Data transferred = 128 bytes

  • Transfer size = 1 byte per DMA transfer

Step 1: Number of DMA transfers

Since DMA transfers 1 byte at a time,

Number of transfers = 128 bytes

Step 2: Time for one DMA bus usage

For each byte transferred:

  • Bus control from CPU to DMA = 250 ns

  • One bus cycle for data transfer = 500 ns

  • Bus control back from DMA to CPU = 250 ns

Time per transfer = 250 + 500 + 250
                  = 1000 ns
                  = 1 μs

Step 3: Total bus tie-up time

Total time = 128 × 1 μs
           = 128 μs

Answer: (128us)

Note: The 50 KB/s device transfer rate is not needed for calculating the bus tie-up time. It only determines how frequently DMA requests occur, not how long the bus is occupied for each DMA transfer.

While executing the ISR, the processor takes about $8 \mu \mathrm{~s}$ for the transfer of each byte. Determine what percentage of processor time is consumed by this I/O device in this case. Given:

- Buffer size = 16 bytes
- Interrupt overhead = 100 μs
- Time to transfer one byte in ISR = 8 μs
- 1 KB = 1000 bytes

Step 1: Calculate the number of interrupts per second

Interrupts/second = 8000 ÷ 16
                  = 500 interrupts/second

Step 2: Calculate the time taken by one interrupt

Interrupt overhead = 100 μs

Time to copy 16 bytes = 16 × 8 μs
                       = 128 μs

Total ISR time = 100 + 128
               = 228 μs

Processor time = 500 × 228 μs
               = 114000 μs

Since 1 second = 1,000,000 μs,

Processor utilization = (114000 ÷ 1,000,000) × 100
                      = 11.4%

Final Answer:

The I/O device consumes 11.40% of the processor time.

questions.html:
A certain microprocessor requires $4.5~\mu s$ to respond to an interrupt. Assume that the three interrupts $I_1$, $I_2$, and $I_3$ require the following execution times after the interrupt is recognized:

  1. $I_1$ requires $25$ microseconds
     
  2. $I_2$ requires $35$ microseconds
     
  3. $I_3$ requires $20$ microseconds

$I_1$ has the highest priority and $I_3$ has the lowest priority. What is the possible range of time for $I_3$ to be executed, assuming that it may or may not occur simultaneously with the other interrupts?

options.html: $24.5$ microseconds to $39.5$ microseconds
$24.5$ microseconds to $93.5$ microseconds
$4.5$  microseconds to $24.5$ microseconds
$29.5$ microseconds to $93.5$ microseconds

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

1. Calculate minimum execution time
 

\(\text{Minimum\ Time}=\text{Response\ Time}+\text{Execution\ Time\ of\ }I_{3}\)
\(\text{Minimum\ Time}=4.5\text{\ }\mu \text{s}+20\text{\ }\mu \text{s}=24.5\text{\ }\mu \text{s}\) 

2. Calculate maximum execution time
 

\(\text{Maximum\ Time}=(\text{Response\ Time}+I_{1})+(\text{Response\ Time}+I_{2})+(\text{Response\ Time}+I_{3})\)
\(\text{Maximum\ Time}=(4.5\text{\ }\mu \text{s}+25\text{\ }\mu \text{s})+(4.5\text{\ }\mu \text{s}+35\text{\ }\mu \text{s})+(4.5\text{\ }\mu \text{s}+20\text{\ }\mu \text{s})\)
\(\text{Maximum\ Time}=29.5\text{\ }\mu \text{s}+39.5\text{\ }\mu \text{s}+24.5\text{\ }\mu \text{s}=93.5\text{\ }\mu \text{s}\)            

Combining these bounds yields a possible range of \(24.5\text{ }\mu\text{s}\) to \(93.5\text{ }\mu\text{s}\)

questions.html:
A DMA controller transfers $16$ -bit words to memory using cycle stealing. The words are assembled from a device that transmits characters at a rate of $2400$ characters per second. The CPU is fetching and executing instructions at an average rate of $1$ million instructions per second. By how much percentage will the CPU be slowed down because of the DMA transfer?

  1. $0.06$
     
  2. $0.12$
     
  3. $1.2$
     
  4. $2.5$
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

1. Calculate Total Bits Transmitted per Second

A standard character equals 1 byte, which consists of 8 bits.
\(\text{Data\ Rate}=2400\text{\ characters/sec}\times 8\text{\ bits/character}=19,200\text{\ bits/sec}\)

 

2. Convert Data Rate to Words per Second

The Direct Memory Access (DMA) controller transfers data in blocks of 16-bit words.
\(\text{DMA\ Word\ Rate}=\frac{19,200\text{\ bits/sec}}{16\text{\ bits/word}}=1200\text{\ words/sec}\)

3. Determine Cycles Stolen by DMA

Under the cycle stealing mode, the DMA controller temporarily pauses the CPU and "steals" exactly 1 bus cycle (equivalent to 1 instruction time) to transfer each word.
\(\text{Cycles\ stolen\ per\ second}=1200\text{\ cycles/sec}\) 

4. Calculate CPU Slowdown Percentage

The CPU normally processes at an average rate of 1 million (\(1,000,000\)) instructions per second.
\(\text{Slowdown\ Percentage}=\left(\frac{\text{Cycles\ Stolen}}{\text{Total\ CPU\ Cycles}}\right)\times 100\)
\(\text{Slowdown\ Percentage}=\left(\frac{1200}{1,000,000}\right)\times 100=0.12\%\)
